content:
Yesterday we studied what happened at Taberah. Israel had only recently begun their journey from Sinai, but the hardship of the wilderness exposed what was in their hearts. Instead of trusting Yahweh, they began to murmur. Yahweh heard their words, His anger was kindled, and fire burned among the outer parts of the camp. When the people cried to Moses, he prayed for them, and the fire was quenched. Today let us consider the lessons this incident gives to us, the New Creation.

The journey of Israel through the wilderness represents the narrow way in which the followers of Christ are called to walk. Christ said, "Narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it" (Matthew 7:14).

The narrow way is not evil, and God has not designed it to destroy us. It is the road that leads to life. Yet it is certainly a hard road, because it requires us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Christ. He said, "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me" (Luke 9:23). And the difficulty of this path is not mainly because of the physical road before us. It is hard because, while we are walking on it, we are being required to develop and reflect the character of Christ.

It is easy to behave well when everyone treats us well. It is easy to speak kindly when others speak kindly to us. But the true character of Christ is revealed when we are hated, misunderstood, betrayed, insulted, or treated unfairly. Christ said, "If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you" (John 15:18). If we truly reflect His character, the spirit of this world will not always accept us. Christ spoke the truth, walked in righteousness, exposed darkness, and obeyed His Father, and therefore the world hated Him. In the same way, those who sincerely follow Christ may face rejection, accusation, misunderstanding, and persecution. This is one reason the narrow way is hard.

Christ also commanded us, "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you" (Matthew 5:44). It is very difficult to love those who hate us. It is difficult to pray for those who have hurt us. It is difficult to show kindness toward someone who has betrayed our trust. Yet this is the very character Christ asks us to develop. In the same way, it is difficult to forgive and forget the painful events of our lives. We may forgive a person sincerely, yet the memory of the betrayal, the argument, the humiliation, or the loss may continue to trouble the mind. Forgiveness can be given in a moment, but the healing of the memory may take time. The Scripture does not command us to pretend that nothing happened. Rather, it commands us not to hold hatred, not to seek revenge, and not to keep counting the offence against the person.

Paul says, "Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye" (Colossians 3:13). And again, he tells us that love "thinketh no evil" (1 Corinthians 13:5).

Therefore the road is filled with trials. Every difficult person, every betrayal, every disappointment, every delay, and every painful circumstance can test whether the character of Christ is truly being formed within us. Peter says,

"The trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire" (1 Peter 1:7). The trials are not meant to make us bitter. They are permitted in order to refine us. But if we fail to understand their purpose, we may begin to murmur, just as Israel did. We may murmur when our prayers are not answered quickly. We may murmur when others do not recognise our sacrifices. We may murmur when the brethren disappoint us.We may murmur when the narrow way becomes lonely, when the battle against sin becomes tiring, or when we face the same difficult lesson again and again. And sometimes we may not murmur openly, but the complaint continues quietly within the heart. Yet Yahweh hears not only the words spoken by the mouth; He also sees the thoughts and the attitudes within us.

Israel's murmuring at Taberah was serious because it suggested that God had not treated them well. They had forgotten His earlier deliverance, His provision, and His presence. In the same way, when we continually murmur, we may forget how Yahweh has already led us, protected us, forgiven us, and blessed us. Paul warns us plainly, "Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer" (1 Corinthians 10:10).If we continue in murmuring without repentance, correction can come.At Taberah, that correction appeared in the form of fire. The fire began in the outer parts of the camp and became a warning to the whole congregation.For us, the fire may not always be a literal flame. It may appear as painful correction, as exposure, as a loss of peace, as damaged relationships, or as circumstances through which Yahweh awakens us to our wrong condition.

However, we must be careful here. We must not say that every trouble in life is proof of God’s anger. Christ and the apostles suffered many trials even while they were completely faithful. Some trials test us, some correct us, and some come simply because we live in a fallen world. Therefore, when things begin to fall apart around us, we should not immediately condemn ourselves or others. But we should humbly examine our hearts before Yahweh. As the Scripture says, "Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to Yahweh" (Lamentations 3:40). If we recognise that we have been murmuring, becoming bitter, or resisting God’s dealings with us, then we must not continue in that condition. We must remember Taberah. We must return to God, confess our wrong attitude, and ask for His forgiveness.

The people at Taberah cried to Moses, and Moses prayed to Yahweh, and the fire was quenched. For the New Creation, we have one who is greater than Moses; Christ himself. "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5). And He "ever liveth to make intercession for them" (Hebrews 7:25). When the narrow way becomes hard, the best thing is not to murmur, but to seek help from our greater Moses, Christ. We can ask Him for strength to endure, for grace to forgive, for power to love our enemies, and for wisdom to face the trial in the right way. Even after repeated warnings, some may still continue to murmur. Israel had seen the cloud, the manna, the Red Sea, and the glory of Yahweh, and yet they still complained. This shows us that knowledge alone does not guarantee faithfulness. We must guard our hearts daily.

The people at the outer parts of the camp became a warning to everyone else. Their judgment taught the whole congregation that murmuring was not a small matter. In the same way, when we see the sad consequences of bitterness, rebellion, and continual complaining in the lives of others, we should not become proud. We should receive it as a warning and examine ourselves.

And if anyone today feels that they are in the midst of severe correction; if peace has departed, if relationships are breaking, if bitterness is increasing, or if life appears to be burning around them; this is the time to stop and return to Yahweh. We should not continue murmuring inside the fire. Let us confess our wrong attitude. Let us ask God for forgiveness through Christ. Let us ask our greater Moses to intercede for us. And let us pray that the fire of correction may accomplish its purpose and then be quenched.

Taberah teaches us that Yahweh hears our murmuring, but it also teaches us that He hears intercession. Judgment came, but mercy was still available.

The fire burned, but it was also quenched. Therefore let us not murmur in the narrow way. Let us remember that the road is hard because it is forming the character of Christ within us. Let us love those who hate us, forgive those who betray us, endure the trials permitted in our lives, and seek help from Christ whenever our strength becomes weak. Then the wilderness will not become our place of destruction. It will become the very place where the character of Christ is completed within us.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,

We confess that the narrow way is hard, and that our hearts are quick to complain.

Forgive us for the murmuring of our lips, and for the quiet complaining we hide within.

Help us to remember how You have already led us, provided for us, and forgiven us.

Teach us to love those who hate us, to forgive those who wound us, and to endure the trials You permit.

When we find ourselves inside the fire, keep us from murmuring, and turn our hearts back to You.

We thank You for our greater Moses, Christ, who ever lives to intercede for us.

Let the wilderness be not our destruction, but the place where the character of Christ is completed in us.

"Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me, and know my thoughts." - Psalm 139:23

In the name of Christ, our Mediator and Intercessor, we pray. Amen.
